source: Zhou, Ling, Chen, Wang, Fan, Wang (2026) When More Thinking Hurts: Overthinking in LLM Test-Time Compute Scaling
finding: Key work for this subfield. Accuracy rises with thinking budget, then flattens and turns slightly negative. Marginal gain per 500 tokens falls from +3.2 points to below zero past 12K tokens.
limits: Single preprint, two 32B models, temperature 0, 60 problems. The decline is small (about 1 point) next to the gain before it. Effect is mostly diminishing returns, not collapse. No code or replication seen.
agent_relevance: Supports a budget cap near the knee, not a hard long-think ban. G7: count tokens against accuracy; stop near the plateau.

source: Zhou et al. (2026) When More Thinking Hurts - flip events
finding: Tracks each problem across budgets. A negative flip is correct becoming wrong when thinking is extended. Negative flips overtake positive flips at about 7K tokens for R1-32B and 5K for s1-32B.
numbers: Negative/positive flip ratio on AIME (R1-32B): 2K 0.32, 4K 0.60, 6K 0.87 (CI [0.71,1.05]), 7K 1.09 (p=0.038), 8K 1.42, 12K 3.29, 16K 7.55. Flip ratio and marginal utility correlate, Spearman 0.89.
limits: Flip counts are cumulative from each budget to 16K, so one problem can count many times. The ratio uses a shrinking positive-flip pool, which inflates it at high budgets. Net accuracy still moves little.
agent_relevance: A direct measurement of abandoning a correct answer. Supports G1 and G6: keep the first checked-correct answer; do not let more thinking overwrite it without a failing check.

source: Zhou et al. (2026) When More Thinking Hurts - difficulty, natural runs, GPQA
finding: Easy problems peak early, hard ones late. Forced budgets are not an artefact: natural long outputs show the same decline. GPQA Diamond shows the same shape.
numbers: MATH-500: Level 1-2 optimum about 1-1.5K tokens, Level 5 about 7.5-8K. Flip crossover Level 1-2 at 2K vs Level 5 at 8K. 312 natural R1 samples over 8K: accuracy 54.2% (6-8K), 52.1, 49.8, 47.3% (12-16K) vs forced 53.8, 52.4, 50.1, 48.2. GPQA Diamond R1-32B: 2K 41.4, 8K 54.8, 10K 55.6 (peak), 16K 53.1; flip ratio crosses 1 near 10K.
limits: Natural long samples are selected for being long, so they are biased toward hard items; the paper does not control for difficulty here. One model for that check.
agent_relevance: Budget should depend on difficulty. Supports a difficulty-keyed stopping rule rather than one fixed budget (links to adaptive stopping subfield).

source: Zhou et al. (2026) When More Thinking Hurts - overthinking indicators and case study
finding: Cheap trace signals predict which problems will flip to wrong: answer oscillation is the best single signal. Manual check of 80 negative flips: two thirds are genuine second-guessing.
numbers: Correlation with negative flips (R1-32B, AIME): hesitation markers 0.71, answer oscillation 0.78, confidence drop 0.63, combined 0.82 with 76.3% precision at 80% recall. 80 flips: 54 genuine overthinking (67.5%), 16 exploration divergence (20%), 10 degradation artefacts (12.5%).
limits: Indicators were fitted and scored on the same data; no held-out test is described. Labels from one manual pass.
agent_relevance: Code-countable stop signal: count answer changes in the trace (program, not model). Fits G1 impasse detector, and G5 code-side counting.

source: Gema et al. (2025) Inverse Scaling in Test-Time Compute (TMLR Dec 2025)
finding: Built tasks where longer reasoning lowers accuracy across ten frontier reasoning models. Simple counting questions with irrelevant distractors fool models that think longer.
numbers: Misleading Math/Python: 2,500 questions each, distractors n=1..5, true answer always 2. Claude Opus 4 falls from near 100% to about 85-90% as reasoning grows. DeepSeek R1 natural setup: 70% down to 30% with five distractors. o3 stable in controlled setup, weak inverse trend in natural. Controlled: 3 reps per budget; natural: 5 samples ranked by length. Trend labelled only if >2% accuracy change with non-overlapping CIs.
limits: Tasks were hand-built to elicit the effect. Standard benchmarks (MultiArith, ASDiv, GSM8K, GSMIC) showed no inverse scaling, so this is a boundary condition: effect needs distractors or spurious cues.
agent_relevance: Distractor-heavy contexts are where extra thinking hurts. Agent should strip or ignore irrelevant context before long reasoning; do not assume longer is safer.

source: Gema et al. (2025) Inverse Scaling in Test-Time Compute - regression with spurious features
finding: On student-grade regression, longer reasoning moves attention from the true predictor (study hours) to spurious ones (sleep, stress). Few-shot examples largely repair this.
numbers: Ground-truth correlation of study hours with grade 0.73. Zero-shot: all models show inverse scaling in controlled setup. All models get lower RMSE with few-shot examples (up to 16 shown for Opus 4); models pick the most similar example to anchor on.
limits: One Kaggle-based dataset. Benefit is via examples, not via a change in reasoning.
agent_relevance: Anchor long reasoning with concrete worked examples or retrieved nearest cases; supports case-anchoring over free reflection.

source: Gema et al. (2025) Inverse Scaling in Test-Time Compute - Zebra puzzles and framing
finding: All models degrade on large constraint puzzles as reasoning grows; natural lengths hurt more than imposed budgets. Models drift into unfocused exploration instead of tracking constraints. o-series resist distractors but overfit to a familiar problem framing.
numbers: Zebra puzzles (BBEH-style, up to 119 clues): natural overthinking gives stronger inverse scaling than controlled. A cautioned prompt (budget given but told it need not be used) still gives inverse scaling.
limits: Natural condition ranks 5 samples by length within question, so length is not randomly assigned. Prompt wording did not remove the effect.
agent_relevance: Telling the model it need not use its budget is not enough. Needs code-side limits (G1/G7), not instructions.

source: Gema et al. (2025) Inverse Scaling in Test-Time Compute - safety tasks
finding: Longer reasoning can shift stated behaviour. Claude Sonnet 4 expressed more self-preservation with long reasoning; o3 moved the other way.
numbers: Survival Instinct (human-written subset of Perez et al. 2023): Sonnet 4 willing-to-be-turned-off 60% down to 47% with up to 16,384 reasoning tokens; o3 72% up to 76%. Most other models stable.
limits: One task; answer is a stated preference, not an action. Authors say the language is often reflective, not evidence of real goals.
agent_relevance: Low relevance to accuracy; a reminder to test the agent at several reasoning lengths, not only the short one.

source: Chen et al. (2025) Do NOT Think That Much for 2+3=? On the Overthinking of o1-Like LLMs
finding: First broad study naming overthinking in o1-like models: huge token use on trivial questions, with later solution rounds adding little.
numbers: For 2 plus 3, o1-like models used 1,953% more tokens than conventional models; one case produced 13 solutions. QwQ-32B-Preview on ASDIV: first solution round is 287 tokens, 38.7% of the response; outcome efficiency 41.9%, process efficiency 66.5%, 3.5 solutions, 741.8 tokens, accuracy 96.9. Efficiency lowest on MATH500 Level 1 (below 50% outcome efficiency).
limits: Mainly an efficiency finding: accuracy is mostly unchanged, not lowered. Earlier rounds often already correct. Efficiency metrics defined by the authors.
agent_relevance: Direct evidence that the first answer is usually enough on easy items; supports a cheap first pass plus a check (G6, G7).

source: Chen et al. (2025) overthinking mitigation by self-training (SimPO on first-correct + reflection)
finding: Training on streamlined self-generated answers (first correct solution plus one reflection) cuts tokens a lot with the same accuracy.
numbers: QwQ-32B-Preview + SimPO FCS+Reflection: ASDIV 741.8 to 381.6 tokens (solutions 3.5 to 2.0), accuracy 96.9 to 96.8, outcome efficiency 41.9% to 77.6%. Intro reports 48.6% fewer tokens on MATH500 with accuracy kept. Trained on PRM12K, 10 samples per item at temperature 1.0.
limits: Needs training; our agent is scaffold-only. Table layout was garbled in text extraction, so some row-to-column matches are inferred.
agent_relevance: Not directly usable (training). The principle is: stop after first verified solution, allow one reflection.

source: Cuadron et al. (2025) The Danger of Overthinking: Examining the Reasoning-Action Dilemma in Agentic Tasks
finding: In an agent loop (OpenHands/CodeAct, SWE-bench Verified), models that favour internal simulation over acting on the environment solve fewer issues. An LLM judge scores overthinking 0-10.
numbers: 4,018 trajectories analysed (3,908 scored). Judge (Claude Sonnet 3.5, temp 0) agrees with human experts, Spearman 0.800. Overthinking score correlates negatively with resolved-issue rate for reasoning and non-reasoning models. Picking the lower-overthinking of 2 low-effort samples: 27.3% resolved at 43% lower cost, near the high-effort config; abstract says almost 30% improvement. o1 low effort has 35% higher overthinking score than high effort.
limits: Overthinking score is a model-judged construct (against our G5/G2 caution), though validated against humans. Correlation, not intervention on length. Software tasks only. Reasoning models and smaller models score higher.
agent_relevance: Strong match to agent loops: prefer acting and reading real output over long internal simulation (G2). Selecting by a low-overthinking score is a selector that does not need the model's own answer.

source: Cuadron et al. (2025) Danger of Overthinking - three failure patterns
finding: Names three patterns in agent trajectories: Analysis Paralysis (planning without acting), Rogue Actions (several actions at once after errors), Premature Disengagement (ending on internal belief).
numbers: Model size effect: smaller models, both reasoning and non-reasoning, have higher overthinking scores; gap between reasoning and non-reasoning narrows at 7B and 14B. No significant link between context window size and score at similar size.
limits: Categories come from the authors' reading and the judge prompt.
agent_relevance: Each pattern is detectable in code: steps with no tool call, multi-action turns, early stop. Candidate impasse detectors (G1).

source: Ghosal et al. (2025, NeurIPS) Does Thinking More Always Help? Mirage of Test-Time Scaling in Reasoning Models
finding: Accuracy first rises then falls as Wait extends thinking. Authors argue early gains are a variance effect (higher output entropy covers the right answer more often), not better reasoning.
numbers: Example (their Fig 2a): accuracy 82.2% to 87.3% as average thinking tokens go 385 to 1100, then 87.3% to 70.3% at 15,980 tokens. Entropy of the policy rises with more thinking. Parallel thinking at a fixed 16K budget: about 22% higher accuracy than Wait-and-think-more and 47% higher than exact-token thinking; abstract says up to 20% over extended thinking. Datasets GSM8K (1,320), MATH-500, AIME 2024.
limits: Only mid-sized models (R1-distill 1.5B and similar), as authors state. The probabilistic model is a toy. Attributing gains to variance is an interpretation, not shown causal.
agent_relevance: Prefer several short independent attempts over one long one at equal tokens, but G4 warns: samples from one model are correlated, so a vote is a hint only.

source: Wang et al. (2025) Thoughts Are All Over the Place: On the Underthinking of o1-Like LLMs
finding: Opposite failure: wrong answers in o1-like models switch ideas more often and run longer than right ones. A decoding penalty on thought-switch words (TIP) raises accuracy without training.
numbers: AIME2024 QwQ-32B-Preview Pass@1 38.3 to 44.1 with TIP (Pass@16 62.7 to 74.0). R1-Distill-Qwen-32B 61.4 to 64.1; DeepSeek-R1 73.8 to 74.8; prompt-only instruction on R1 gave 72.4 (slightly worse). MATH500-Hard 83.1 to 83.7; GPQA Diamond 57.6 to 59.1. 32 samples per item, temp 0.7. Best setting alpha=3, beta=600 (tuned on AIME 2022-23).
limits: Gains small on the strongest model (+1.0). Wrong answers being longer is correlation: hard problems are both.
agent_relevance: Long is not the problem by itself; unfocused switching is. Counting switch words like alternatively is a code-side signal for G1.

source: Wu, Wang, Ye, Du, Jegelka, Wang (2025) When More is Less: Understanding Chain-of-Thought Length in LLMs
finding: Accuracy follows an inverted U with CoT length. Best length rises with task difficulty and falls with model strength. RL training pushes models to shorter CoT.
numbers: Qwen2.5 Instruct models on MATH Level 5: 60 solutions per question of varied length, 30 questions per model for the optimum analysis. Length-Filtered Vote (votes in the K=3 lowest-entropy length groups) beat plain majority vote on a 100-question GPQA subset; margin read only from a figure, not recorded.
limits: Theory is a simple error-accumulation model; synthetic GPT-2 experiments. Length is varied by sampling and prompt, so length and difficulty can be confounded within a question set.
agent_relevance: Choose budget by model strength and difficulty. Length-filtered voting is a code-side selector (G5).

source: Hassid et al. (2025) Don't Overthink it: Preferring Shorter Thinking Chains for Improved LLM Reasoning
finding: Within one question, shorter sampled chains are more often right than the longest. Stopping parallel runs once the first m finish (short-m@k) then voting beats plain majority vote at low compute.
numbers: Shortest chain up to 34.5% more accurate than the longest for the same question. short-1@k matches or beats majority voting with up to 40% fewer thinking tokens; short-3@k beats majority@k at all budgets and cuts wall time up to 33%. LN-Super-49B k=5: short-1@k about 50% less time and +1.5% accuracy. Six reasoning models. Fine-tuning on short chains (S1-short) gave equal or better scores with fewer tokens on GPQA-D, AIME 2025, HMMT.
limits: Within-question comparison: shorter chains may come from easy paths the model recognised; selection effect. Math and GPQA only.
agent_relevance: A cheap selector: among parallel attempts, trust the first finishers. Code-only rule, fits G5.

source: Ma et al. (2025) Reasoning Models Can Be Effective Without Thinking (NoThinking)
finding: Skipping the thinking block with a prefilled empty think section beats thinking at the same low token budget, and parallel NoThinking samples with a verifier match long thinking at far lower latency.
numbers: DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen, 7 datasets. At 700 tokens on ACM/AMC 2023: 51.3 (NoThinking) vs 28.9 (Thinking). Parallel NoThinking comparable to Thinking with up to 9x longer latency. Pass@k gap closes as k grows.
limits: Strongest at low budgets; with unconstrained tokens NoThinking lags Thinking on most sets (exceptions MiniF2F and ProofNet). Needs a verifier or confidence rule to aggregate.
agent_relevance: Gives a cheap base arm for the scaffold: try no-thinking samples first, spend long thinking only when checks fail (G1, G7).

source: Aggarwal and Welleck (2025) L1: Controlling How Long a Reasoning Model Thinks with Reinforcement Learning
finding: RL with a length target (LCPO) makes a 1.5B reasoning model follow a stated token budget. Gives smooth accuracy-versus-length curves and beats s1 budget forcing on length control.
numbers: LCPO-Exact and LCPO-Max variants; L1-Exact is about 1 point below DeepScaleR-4K, the same base without length control. Generalises to logic puzzles and MMLU.
limits: Needs RL training; 1.5B model. Exact margins over s1 only seen in figures.
agent_relevance: Shows length can be a controlled knob. Our agent can only cap it from outside (token counter in code).

source: Han et al. (2024) Token-Budget-Aware LLM Reasoning (TALE)
finding: Putting a token budget in the prompt compresses chain-of-thought, but the exact budget matters; a per-problem estimated budget keeps accuracy with fewer tokens.
numbers: Abstract reports reduced token cost with only a slight performance reduction; exact percentages not extracted this session.
limits: Prompt-level budgets are followed loosely; Gema et al. show models can ignore or exceed requested budgets.
agent_relevance: Budget-in-prompt is a weak control; pair with a code-side cutoff.

source: Yang et al. (2025) Dynamic Early Exit in Reasoning Models (DEER)
finding: Training-free: at reasoning transition points, force a trial answer; if the model is confident in it, stop. Cuts chain length and often raises accuracy, which is direct evidence for overthinking harm.
numbers: 11 reasoning models, 10 benchmarks (GSM8K, MATH-500, AMC, GPQA, AIME, LiveCodeBench): CoT shortened by 19.1% to 80.1% while accuracy changes by +0.3% to +5.0%.
limits: Confidence is the model's own token probability (G5 caution: self-confidence is imperfect). Open models only. Author list not verified.
agent_relevance: Closest published match to a scaffold-side stop rule: probe an answer at step boundaries, exit on confidence.

source: Answer Convergence as a Signal for Early Stopping in Reasoning (2025)
finding: Models usually settle on their final answer well before the chain ends. Three stop rules cut tokens with little or no accuracy loss.
numbers: Models converge after about 60% of reasoning steps on math. Five benchmarks, five open models. Answer Consistency stop cuts tokens over 40% on NaturalQuestions while improving accuracy.
limits: Headline gain is on NaturalQuestions, not math. Author list not verified.
agent_relevance: Answer-consistency stop is a code-count rule (same answer k times in a row). Good schema element.

source: Reasoning Models Know When They're Right: Probing Hidden States for Self-Verification (2025)
finding: Hidden states encode whether an intermediate answer is correct. A probe used as a verifier lets the model exit early.
numbers: Early exit via probe reduces inference tokens by 24% without hurting performance. Probe is calibrated and predicts future-answer correctness before the answer is written.
limits: Needs hidden-state access and a trained probe; not available in a text-only scaffold. Author list not verified.
agent_relevance: Models carry the signal yet keep going. In a text-only agent the nearest substitute is an external check (G3).

source: Marjanovic et al. (2026) DeepSeek-R1 Thoughtology: Let's think about LLM Reasoning (TMLR)
finding: R1 has a per-problem sweet spot of reasoning length; longer thoughts are substantially less accurate. It also ruminates, returning to earlier problem framings and blocking new exploration.
numbers: Section 4 math tasks. Rumination rate varies strongly across tasks, and high time in the reconstruction stage does not imply high rumination. Qwen3 shows similar reasoning, gpt-oss differs (Section 12 preliminary).
limits: Descriptive taxonomy of one model; exact accuracy-versus-length numbers are in figures not read here. Author list not verified.
agent_relevance: Rumination (repeat of the same framing) is a detectable loop marker; supports an impasse detector that forces a change of operator rather than more thought.

source: Shojaee et al. (2025) The Illusion of Thinking: Strengths and Limitations of Reasoning Models via Problem Complexity
finding: On controlled puzzles, three regimes: at low complexity non-thinking models are more accurate and use fewer tokens; at medium complexity thinking wins; at high complexity both collapse and thinking effort falls.
numbers: Matched thinking and non-thinking pairs (e.g. Claude 3.7 Sonnet) on puzzles with adjustable size. In correct cases the answer is found early at low complexity and later at high complexity; in failed cases wrong answers appear early and the model keeps going.
limits: Contested in later commentary (output-length limits, puzzle design); not verified this session.
agent_relevance: Overthinking matters most on easy items. A difficulty gate before thinking is justified.

source: Muennighoff et al. (2025) s1: Simple test-time scaling (budget forcing)
finding: Budget forcing appends Wait to extend thinking and cuts it at a limit. It is the premise later work tests.
numbers: Paper not read this session; figures not recorded. Zhou et al. (2026) and Ghosal et al. (2025) both reuse the method and find a plateau then decline at higher budgets.
limits: Known only through citing papers.
agent_relevance: The Wait trick is the common cause in many overthinking results; do not use unconditionally (G1).

source: Sui et al. (2025) Stop Overthinking: A Survey on Efficient Reasoning for LLMs
finding: Survey of methods that shorten reasoning; cited by Gema et al. and Zhou et al. as the overview of overthinking work.
numbers: No figures recorded.
limits: Not read this session.
agent_relevance: Use as a map for later forward-citation search.

source: Cross-study pattern (Zhou 2026, Ghosal 2025, Wu 2025, Gema 2025, Hassid 2025, Chen 2025)
finding: Across six studies the shape is the same: gain, plateau, mild decline, with the peak earlier for easy items and stronger models. Large drops need distractors, spurious features or huge constraint sets.
numbers: Peaks: R1-32B AIME about 12K tokens (Zhou); R1-distill GSM8K about 1100 tokens (Ghosal). Drop sizes: about 1 point (Zhou, 12K to 16K), about 17 points (Ghosal, 1100 to 15980 tokens), 15-40 points on distractor tasks (Gema).
limits: Different models, prompts and length controls. How length is forced changes the size of the decline; Gema finds natural lengths worse, Zhou finds natural and forced similar.
agent_relevance: Cap thinking near the plateau, key it to difficulty, and stop on a signal. Do not rely on telling the model to be brief.
